The Maintainers Summit is a one-day, invitation-only gathering of about 30 kernel developers; it is held once each year to discuss policy-related issues that are not always amenable to resolution via email. The 2026 event was scheduled for October 8 in Prague, Czechia. Unsurprisingly, the discussion there was dominated by large language models (LLMs) and their effect on the development community, but some time was also found to talk about security bugs and long-term succession planning.

Unlike previous years, the 2026 Summit did not have a well-defined schedule with specific developers identified to lead the discussion on each topic. The conversation was rather more free-flowing, and this writeup will match that structure (or lack thereof). Some minimal reordering has been done in an attempt to provide a more coherent overview.

TL;DR

For those who do not want to plow through all that follows, here is a summary of the most significant conclusions. Please note that this is entirely my interpretation; it is not any sort of official communication from the Summit.

  • Sashiko no longer reports pre-existing bugs found when reviewing patches; the reaction to this change was mixed. Sashiko is appreciated, but some maintainers fear it fuels the rapid tweak-and-resend cycle that new submitters tend to fall into.
  • Linus Torvalds believes that blaming LLMs for the kernel community's problems is wrong, when the problem is LLM users who do not understand how to use them or how the kernel works. A properly trained LLM is a useful tool, but it takes a lot of time to reach that point.
  • Torvalds and others repeatedly said low-quality contributions from new developers should receive low priority, and that the community should stop trying to make contribution easy. Many developers said, repeatedly, that trying to mentor those developers is almost always a waste of time; they do not listen.
  • There is some concern about companies maintaining private kernels with LLM help, but there does not seem to be much to be done about it.
  • Kernel developers should not be required to use LLMs to work in the community, but those who do need to have enough resources available to generate acceptable results.
  • The requirement to add Assisted-by tags to patches created with LLMs will be removed, but maintainers still want to know about how a patch was created.
  • The development community is struggling to keep up with the flood of security patches, and will continue to for some time. Some of the most urgent fixes may bypass maintainers and go straight to Torvalds. Maintainers were cautioned against telling their employers about vulnerabilities before public disclosure happens.
  • The maintainers each briefly presented an aspect of the development process that causes them pain; many talked about the review process, keeping up with the load, and submitters who are not interested in learning.
  • Torvalds said that the community should start thinking more about how leadership succession should work so that there will be a plan in place when, some years from now, he decides to retire.

Sashiko and patch review

The initial topic was automated patch review, and the Sashiko review system in particular. When Sashiko is looking at a specific patch, it often identifies (and reports on) problems that already exist in the code that is modified by that patch. Developers have a love-and-hate relationship with the resulting reports; it is good to know about the bugs, but nobody is thrilled to be given a laundry list of problems in need of fixing, especially if it is seen as an obstacle that must be overcome before they can merge the changes they actually intended to implement.

Recently, Sashiko developer Roman Gushchin announced that pre-existing bugs would no longer be included in patch reviews; instead, they will be stored into a separate database and made available to maintainers. Ted Ts'o started the Summit discussion by mentioning this change, noting that there is a large backlog of problems that no longer appear in Sashiko reviews. Peter Zijlstra asked why this change was made, since it is still important to know about those bugs; Gushchin answered that the bugs are still being detected, but they are hidden from the reports and set aside waiting for somebody to deal with them.

Christoph Hellwig said that it would be better to keep the pre-existing problems in the patch review, but perhaps mark them differently so that submitters know they are not required to address them. Old problems should not be forced onto new submitters, he said. Mark Brown agreed, saying that submitters should not have to fix a structural problem in order to get a spelling fix in. Hellwig added that removing the pre-existing items is worse, since they are problems that need to be fixed eventually. Gushchin repeated that those problems are collected for people who are interested in fixing them.

Zijlstra complained about maintainers who refuse to consider patches until Sashiko reports that it has found no problems. Hellwig, though, said that Sashiko reviews are a good test for submitters; if they know what they are doing, they should be able to explain why a warning is wrong. Thomas Gleixner replied that the worst submitters will just feed the review into their LLM and send the response.

Ts'o suggested that the best practice will differ from one subsystem to the next. In larger subsystems, the sub-maintainers may not have the skills to tell whether a given bug report is valid or not; they are having a harder time dealing with false positives. A small subsystem with expert maintainers handles those reports better. The solution is partly cultural, he said; it is necessary to tell people that they can ignore the pre-existing problems. Dave Airlie suggested splitting the report into two emails, one with the review of the patch and a second listing the pre-existing problems.

Hellwig shifted the topic slightly by complaining that Sashiko drops most of the recipients from its replies; they should go to everybody, he said, or the thread of the discussion will be broken. David Hildenbrand was quick to disagree, though; in the memory-management subsystem, the Sashiko emails are seen as useful for maintainers, but should not be automatically sent back to the submitter or the mailing list. In a complaint that was heard a few times during the day, he said that submitters spend time submitting multiple versions of a patch set that address comments from Sashiko before human reviewers have a chance to say whether the patch makes sense at all. The Sashiko reviews tend to discourage human reviews in general. His suggestion was that Sashiko should be the last line of defense rather than the first; maintainers should say when the automated review happens.

Review practices

That led to a discussion on review practices and when human reviewers should get involved with a submission. Ts'o said that, in the ext4 filesystem, it depends on the size of the series and the reputation of the submitter. A single patch from an unknown contributor is likely to be LLM-generated crap, so it ends up low on the prioritized list of work to review. A larger series, though, requires architectural review, so he tends to look mainly at the cover letter and limit comments to the overall design.

Jiri Kosina said that deprioritizing unknown contributors is too easy of a solution; in his experience, the patches they submit are often valid. Brown said that proximity to the hardware makes a difference, and that one-off patches to low-level code often have little value. Paolo Abeni said that, in the networking subsystem, there is a complicated scheme for prioritizing reviews that depends on the contributor's reputation, how many reviews that contributor has done, and the reputation of the contributor's employer as well. Airlie warned that tracking reputations raises privacy problems and invites developers to game the system; he understands why that approach has appeal, but a better way is needed. Konstantin Ryabitsev agreed that any reputation system will be gamed.

Laurent Pinchart said that some developers are frustrated that they have to justify their work against criticisms from Sashiko while other, LLM-generated patches appear to be accepted immediately. Abeni defended the automated reviews, though, saying that the number of patches introducing bugs has dropped considerably. Zijlstra said that, while reading LLM-generated reviews "shuts my brain down", he still thought that the tool is useful; it finds real problems.

Linus speaks

At this point Torvalds, who had kept silent until now, spoke up. The problem, he said, is that we are getting increasing numbers of patches from people who do not know the kernel. By pointing the finger at LLMs, maintainers are blaming the wrong thing. LLMs can do a good job, but they are being driven by people who have no clue, and the results are ugly. He suggested maybe delaying reports from Sashiko for 24 hours; that will keep clueless developers from getting an immediate response and cranking out new versions of their work.

He has been playing with an LLM on a separate project for several months to learn about the technology, but hadn't used one on the kernel until last week. He took an old patch and had the LLM revise it; the result has made him unwilling to work without an LLM. He plans to post that series at some point. Why bother, he asked, to search for all of the call sites of a function he has just modified, when the tool can fix them all automatically? But, he said, it took six months to set up the tool to not produce bad responses. If you are a competent developer, he said, an LLM makes a great tool, but only after that effort has been put in to set it up. He resisted suggestions to post his LLM-training materials, saying that each developer needs to go through that process separately.

In conclusion, he said, arguments about how to deal with people using LLMs are misdirected; instead, developers should be focused on how to use these tools well. Hildenbrand said that Torvalds is an expert, but that we still have to deal with all of the non-experts who are submitting patches; Torvalds said to simply deprioritize them.

Sasha Levin suggested putting more information into the repository to try to direct the tools; he later posted a first installment toward building up that information. Ts'o said that it would be useful to try to provide better input for the developers who are willing to put in the effort. Alexei Starovoitov, though, answered that it is not the maintainers' job to teach humans how to work on the kernel. The community is teaching bots by way of the mailing lists, though, and that is reinforcing the problems with rapid reposting of patches.

Gushchin said that, eventually, Sashiko may be able to tell a contributor that a patch is a bad idea in general and should not be revised. Greg Kroah-Hartman said that we can expect to be on the receiving end of a firehose for the next 18 months, then we will have fixed most of the bugs and life will get better. Pinchart responded that fixing the bugs is not enough; the kernel is full of bad APIs that are easier to misuse than to use correctly. Kroah-Hartman said that the bugs will eventually be fixed, then there will be space to work on the APIs.

Ryabitsev said that problem is that contributing to the kernel has always been gated; it is too hard for many developers to do successfully. LLMs have made the creation of kernel patches easy. Pinchart said that a lot of LLM-using contributors just want to see their name in the changelog; they are not going to stay around, so any effort put into mentoring them is wasted. Torvalds repeated that maintainers should simply deprioritize those contributions. Hildenbrand asked how that could be done; Zijlstra suggested responding to a patch and seeing whether LLM-generated text comes back. Comments that do not evoke a clear human response can simply be ignored. Kroah-Hartman said that is the value of pointing out trivial items, like include files in the wrong order. Christian Brauner said that overly verbose changelogs are often a sign of LLM use.

Airlie suggested adding guidance for LLMs that prohibits them from writing changelogs. Levin has been trying to add some of that type of guidance for a while; that effort is likely to be pursued further. There was general agreement that, even if the code is written by an LLM, the accompanying changelog should be written by the human behind the work.

Private kernels

Brauner said that the work of the kernel community is changing in fundamental ways, and what it means for Linux is unclear. There is increasing interest at companies in maintaining private forks of the kernel and not bothering with upstream. Zijlstra suggested asking Google how well that works; Gleixner added that the fundamental economics around maintaining a kernel have not changed. Brauner said that the developers in the room had grown up in an environment dominated by open-source software, and that working with it could lead to a good career; if that is no longer the case, why should anybody bother contributing back?

A number of participants suggested that any company wanting to try its luck with a private fork was welcome to do so. Kroah-Hartman said that the community's goal has always been to make it cheaper to work upstream than to maintain private code. Miguel Ojeda asked whether that was still possible; he knows somebody who has used an LLM to summon forth a complete kernel written in Rust. How can working upstream be cheaper than that? Torvalds said that, if it gets to that point, the community may no longer be viable, but that is not the situation now. Starovoitov said he knew of five working kernels that had been generated in this way; Torvalds answered that there is no point in worrying about them.

Tso's said that, if somebody wants to conjure up a fast microkernel for a specific use case, they can do that now, but a general-purpose kernel designed to handle random corner cases is a different story. He thinks that there will be a demand for the Linux kernel for some time yet. Starovoitov stressed the need to understand why there is interest in generating private kernels; Linux, he said, is too full of holes that are not being fixed quickly enough, and contributing to the kernel is too hard.

Too hard, or too easy?

This was my chance to share a couple of anecdotes I had been saving for this gathering. While running on the unending treadmill that is keeping up with the linux-kernel mailing list, I had recently encountered a series of well over 100 patches, all sent within an hour from a new identity, making significant changes all over the kernel tree. When viewed that way, those patches are the obvious output of an unleashed bot and best ignored, but most maintainers only see a few of them, miss the pattern, and attempt to engage seriously with the sender. So many of those patches are applied.

There is an incredible flood of first-time contributors (nearly 800 in 7.3 alone) burying the community in patches. There have been plenty of cases of first-time contributors who make non-trivial changes to multiple subsystems over a short period of time. To me, it is clear that many of these submitters do not understand what they are doing, and they will not be around to fix or maintain those patches. But a lot of that code is getting into the kernel. My fear is that we are building up a collection of code that nobody understands, and that one day we will wake up and find that we have completely lost control of our kernel.

Airlie responded that we never really did have control over it. Torvalds said that the time has come to make it harder for new people to contribute code to the kernel. People like Kroah-Hartman have spent years trying to teach people how to contribute; it is time to stop doing that, he said. Ojeda said that there is a need to deprioritize these contributors, but that we still need to find talented people to join our community. That means finding ways to focus on the people who actually matter. For example, the people who take the time to go to conferences are much more likely to stay around. The vast majority of patches from new contributors are not worth it, but some are, and identifying them is hard.

Shuah Khan said that she can identify the people who will stick around fairly quickly, and some of the new folks who have come in are excellent. For this reason, she still spends a lot of time with people sending spelling fixes. Hellwig said that developers should be able to use whatever tools they want. For any non-trivial work, there will always be problems to fix; at that point, it is a matter of whether it is possible to have a real conversation with the contributor. Abeni, though, objected that this approach does not scale for the larger subsystems.

Generating code

Ojeda raised the topic of where generating code with LLMs makes sense. In the presence of a clear specification and a concrete problem, an LLM can create good results, he said. The tools can be good for trying out concepts; it may not even be necessary to look at the resulting code before tossing it and implementing a successful concept properly. Generating tests is another place where LLMs can do well. Brauner said that LLMs can be good for prototyping.

Hildenbrand said that the discussion had focused on new contributors, which is fine, but how can we let other maintainers know that it is acceptable to ignore patches from those people? Hellwig said that it is always acceptable to ignore patches; I replied that, for many years, we had been working hard to prevent patches from falling through the cracks.

Torvalds suggested adding an AGENTS.md file that makes generating kernel code expensive. He ends every session with a lengthy cleanup pass that takes a couple of hours to run, executing tasks like ensuring that the code matches the comments. That amount of work cannot be done with a free LLM account. I asked whether that risked cutting off bright new developers that we would rather hang onto; Torvalds answered that the kernel project only wants serious developers. That includes having access to enough resources to function in this world.

Pinchart said that he has heard from a number of developers who are afraid that they will be forced out of the community; Torvalds replied that it will always possible to write code and send email. The point is filtering out the people who cannot do that on their own. Pinchart asked Torvalds to confirm that he is not trying to push out developers who do not use LLMs; Torvalds agreed that he is not. Pinchart added that it is important to communicate that message to the community. Torvalds added that he does not want to scare off people who want to write code; his message is that you have to either put in the effort to learn, or put a lot of money into an LLM to participate.

Airlie expressed a concern that there might not be anything left for those people to write; as soon as an idea is raised, somebody can summon an implementation from an LLM. Alice Ryhl agreed that this could be a problem. Ojeda suggested setting up a way to assign a project to a developer for a period; Hellwig said that the only reason to do that would be for training purposes. Otherwise, why wait when there is an implementation ready? Ojeda said that supporting developers who do not want to use LLMs is also a good reason.

Assisted-by

Documentation/process/coding-assistants.rst was added to the 7.0 kernel to provide guidance for developers using these tools; among other things, it calls for an Assisted-by tag to be added to the changelog of patches developed with LLM assistance. The 7.3 kernel has seen 18,533 non-merge changesets (a record) added through -rc7, 1,884 (essentially 10%) of them contain Assisted-by tags. The actual number of LLM-assisted patches is surely much higher.

In the Summit, I pointed out that huge numbers of contributors are not placing those tags despite using LLMs; sometimes that is the result of ignorance of the rules, while other times contributors want to actively hide their LLM use. But few maintainers are asking contributors about LLM use and ensuring that those tags are present. As a result, Assisted-by provides no useful signal. We should either find a way to enforce the requirement, I suggested, or else just drop it entirely.

Airlie said that probably 90% of contributors are using LLMs now. Many of them, he said, fear being caught up in an anti-LLM witch hunt. He suggested adding a requirement that models read all of the kernel's documentation into an AGENTS.md file. Torvalds thought many submitters were simply ashamed to admit that they were using those tools. Gleixner suggested, not entirely seriously, adding a Not-assisted-by tag instead; Arnd Bergmann said he would find that a useful indicator of developers he should put time into helping.

Torvalds said that the tag requirement might scare people away from using LLMs, and that he would be happy to drop the requirement; Brauner added that it is pointless now. Khan said that she still found Assisted-by to be useful, but there was a strong consensus in the room that the tag had outlived any purpose it may have had, and that the requirement could be dropped.

That said, there was also a general interest in knowing how patches are created. Some would like to see which models were used, or where in the development process they were brought in. Maintainers still want to know if there is a human involved in the development process. There was agreement, though, that this information does not need to be recorded in the changelog; the suggestion came out of the discussion is that this information should be put into the cover letter instead.

Security issues and urgent fixes

The advent of LLMs has resulted in the discovery of huge numbers of security-relevant bugs, leading to a lot of fixes. Kroah-Hartman, who plays a central role in responding to those bugs, said that there are many more coming. Current tools find a lot of vulnerabilities, he said, but they are also wrong half the time; he has students working on improving that performance. He also has people and funding to help with handling the resulting fixes. We can work through this pile of problems, he said, but it will take a while. That is what the next year of work will be focused on.

Levin added that LLMs do two things that are new. One is that they are good at developing an exploit from a patch; the other is that they can be used to monitor mailing lists and figure out which fixes have security implications. The result is machines that are automatically cranking out exploits. As soon as a problem has been detected, he said, any embargo is already over. There are thousands of known exploits out there at the moment.

Kroah-Hartman said that the only thing that can be done is to get the fixes into the mainline as quickly as possible. Brauner pointed out that this leads to large pull requests after -rc1, which Torvalds has complained about. Torvalds, though, said that pull requests full of fixes are fine as long as they come from people who he can trust to have verified them to be fixes for real problems. The cost to him of doing a pull is almost zero; it's his job.

Pinchart said that, while fixing bugs is good, what is really needed is ways to prevent the addition of new bugs. Kroah-Hartman said that increased use of Rust would help in that regard; many bugs are in error paths, and Rust has better ways of handling those. There is also an effort to scale up the work on hardening C code. Some of that work is landing in the newest versions of the compilers, but developers often do not have easy access to them, and linux-next does not either. Ojeda said there is work underway to increase the availability of prebuilt toolchains that developers can use to test their code.

Kroah-Hartman said that security bugs are being immediately copied to maintainers now rather than being kept secret; it is the only way to keep up with the flood. But, he cautioned, maintainers should not be telling their employers about those bugs before they are public; otherwise the project as a whole risks running into trouble with government agencies worldwide. Once a fix has been pushed, though, the embargo ends.

Starovoitov said that there are lists of vulnerabilities that have been discovered by LLMs, many of which have reproducers available. He wondered what the best way was to get those fixes into the mainline. Torvalds said that, when there are real kernel developers involved, the most urgent patches can go directly to him, bypassing maintainers and avoiding adding to their workload. Hildenbrand worried that maintainers would lose the opportunity to review fixes in their subsystems, and that they would lose control, but Torvalds answered that reviewing all those fixes just adds stress for everybody involved.

Pain points

Prior to the Summit, Torvalds asked each of the participants to prepare a one-minute summary of their biggest pain point for the group. These presentations would happen over a half hour, with no discussion until everybody had said their piece. The "no discussion" rule held most (but not all) of the time. In the order they were presented:

  • Kroah-Hartman: subsystems that do not add CC: stable@vger.kernel.org tags to patches, but which still expect the stable team to pick up the important fixes anyway. The stable maintainers are overwhelmed as it is and are not doing that.
  • Pinchart has heard from developers that they submit code, but do not know when their patches have been applied or to which tree. More maintainers should send emails when they apply patches, he said.
  • Eric Biggers: patches that cannot easily be applied, and which do not specify a base to which they can be applied. A lot of patches cannot be properly reviewed without applying them first, he said.
  • Rafael Wysocki: insufficient feedback on patches in general. People often have opinions, but do not always share them.
  • Airlie asked his sub-maintainers; most of them identified him as the biggest pain point. More seriously, it was that the DRM subsystem is still seeing too many regressions. There is a push within the subsystem to move development to GitLab in order to use its CI features; he is not standing in the way because he wants to see how it turns out.
  • Ts'o: prioritization, and having too many things to look at. He would love to add a priority tag to patchwork that maintainers could set to help identify what needs attention first.
  • Ryhl: not knowing how long she needs to wait after sending a version of a patch before concluding that she does not need to worry about problems with it.
  • Me: huge number of patches touch the documentation directory, and it is hard to know which ones I should apply and which to leave to others. A lot of time is spent digging through linux-next to see if patches have been picked up by somebody else. Torvalds said that he often has the same problem.
  • Khan complained about the same problem; it is often not clear who will pick up test patches.
  • Hildenbrand: the high review load. Review cannot just be handed off to a bot; most changes need input from developers. Somehow, the subsystem needs to develop more experts, but it is hard to identify people who can grow in that way.
  • Bergmann said that the review process is breaking down. When he replies to patches, he tries to teach contributors how to do better, but he has become discouraged because people using LLMs do not learn. So now those who might learn are not getting the feedback they need. The opposite problem happens too: a submitter sends 50 versions (literally) of a patch and responds to comments, but Bergmann thinks that the patch should not exist in the first place.
  • Starovoitov: maintainers should not be looking for bugs or coding-style problems; bots will do that now. Instead, reviews should be strictly focused on the "why" of a patch, whether the fix is made in the right place, and is in good taste.
  • Ryabitsev: the last entry in the MAINTAINERS file, titled "THE REST", directs every patch to the linux-kernel mailing list. That generates millions of outgoing emails every day, leading to constant delivery problems. He asked whether that entry could be removed or changed to redirect patches to the patches@vger.kernel.org list. He later submitted a patch to get_maintainer.pl, causing it to only add linux-kernel if no other list has been identified as a recipient for a patch.
  • Levin: subsystems are diverging in their practices, and many now have a manual on how to interact with them. That makes life hard for developers working across subsystems; he would like to see the community come back together.
  • Hellwig: the Sashiko review workflow is broken, causing people to continually resend patches. There is no obvious answer to this problem, but something needs to improve.
  • Brown asked subsystems with tests to actually build and run them so they don't break in linux-next.
  • Kosina: there needs to be a better way to prioritize the handling of submissions. He liked Ts'o's idea, but without using patchwork.
  • Will Deacon: the process is not much fun anymore; maintainers try to explain to contributors how they could improve, but are ignored.
  • Danilo Krummrich does not mind seeing multiple versions of a series in a short time, but submitters are just feeding the Sashiko reviews into their LLM to create those new versions. A way needs to be found to encourage submitters to engage and talk to maintainers.
  • Abeni: the infrastructure is not keeping up with what the subsystem needs. Networking runs its own version of Sashiko, which produces better results, but it can't be run for every networking subsystem. That creates extra friction for maintainers.
  • Eric Dumazet announced that he had just retired, and that all of his pain points have vanished.
  • Gushchin: Sashiko has gone from an experiment to a widely used tool in the community. There is a lot of work involved beyond developing the bot itself; he has to obtain tokens to run it, explain its value to management, and more. He could really use more people and more feedback. He only knows a few kernel subsystems; if people don't tell him about problems with the others, he will never know.
  • Julia Lawall does not know if her work, much of which has involved finding and fixing bugs in the kernel, will have any relevance in the future. Five years ago she would have asked for more feedback from developers, now she isn't sure if it matters.
  • Ojeda: tree-wide refactoring work can be tricky, and the advent of more Rust code seems set to make it harder.
  • Gleixner has spent much of his time looking at design patterns and explaining them in lengthy emails. Developers used to appreciate that work, but more recently it is mostly ignored, and he wonders if it is still worth doing. In the LLM world, people say that they don't have time for design and, besides, the code works. He has spent 25 years doing cleanups, and does not want to merge more stuff that will just have to be cleaned up in the future.
  • Brauner: code removal. The time has come to fix less code and to remove more of it.

The idea was that these pain points would be discussed after the presentation, but that did not really happen. Instead, the conversation took a rather different direction.

Succession

Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room.

He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react.

There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model.

No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future.

Metadiscussion

The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole.

Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased.

Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group.

Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times.

The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well.

content_text: Welcome to LWN.net The following subscription-only content has been made available to you by an LWN subscriber. Thousands of subscribers depend on LWN for the best news from the Linux and free software communities. If you enjoy this article, please consider subscribing to LWN. Thank you for visiting LWN.net! The Maintainers Summit is a one-day, invitation-only gathering of about 30 kernel developers; it is held once each year to discuss policy-related issues that are not always amenable to resolution via email. The 2026 event was scheduled for October 8 in Prague, Czechia. Unsurprisingly, the discussion there was dominated by large language models (LLMs) and their effect on the development community, but some time was also found to talk about security bugs and long-term succession planning. Unlike previous years, the 2026 Summit did not have a well-defined schedule with specific developers identified to lead the discussion on each topic. The conversation was rather more free-flowing, and this writeup will match that structure (or lack thereof). Some minimal reordering has been done in an attempt to provide a more coherent overview. TL;DR For those who do not want to plow through all that follows, here is a summary of the most significant conclusions. Please note that this is entirely my interpretation; it is not any sort of official communication from the Summit. Sashiko no longer reports pre-existing bugs found when reviewing patches; the reaction to this change was mixed. Sashiko is appreciated, but some maintainers fear it fuels the rapid tweak-and-resend cycle that new submitters tend to fall into. Linus Torvalds believes that blaming LLMs for the kernel community's problems is wrong, when the problem is LLM users who do not understand how to use them or how the kernel works. A properly trained LLM is a useful tool, but it takes a lot of time to reach that point. Torvalds and others repeatedly said low-quality contributions from new developers should receive low priority, and that the community should stop trying to make contribution easy. Many developers said, repeatedly, that trying to mentor those developers is almost always a waste of time; they do not listen. There is some concern about companies maintaining private kernels with LLM help, but there does not seem to be much to be done about it. Kernel developers should not be required to use LLMs to work in the community, but those who do need to have enough resources available to generate acceptable results. The requirement to add Assisted-by tags to patches created with LLMs will be removed, but maintainers still want to know about how a patch was created. The development community is struggling to keep up with the flood of security patches, and will continue to for some time. Some of the most urgent fixes may bypass maintainers and go straight to Torvalds. Maintainers were cautioned against telling their employers about vulnerabilities before public disclosure happens. The maintainers each briefly presented an aspect of the development process that causes them pain; many talked about the review process, keeping up with the load, and submitters who are not interested in learning. Torvalds said that the community should start thinking more about how leadership succession should work so that there will be a plan in place when, some years from now, he decides to retire. Sashiko and patch review The initial topic was automated patch review, and the Sashiko review system in particular. When Sashiko is looking at a specific patch, it often identifies (and reports on) problems that already exist in the code that is modified by that patch. Developers have a love-and-hate relationship with the resulting reports; it is good to know about the bugs, but nobody is thrilled to be given a laundry list of problems in need of fixing, especially if it is seen as an obstacle that must be overcome before they can merge the changes they actually intended to implement. Recently, Sashiko developer Roman Gushchin announced that pre-existing bugs would no longer be included in patch reviews; instead, they will be stored into a separate database and made available to maintainers. Ted Ts'o started the Summit discussion by mentioning this change, noting that there is a large backlog of problems that no longer appear in Sashiko reviews. Peter Zijlstra asked why this change was made, since it is still important to know about those bugs; Gushchin answered that the bugs are still being detected, but they are hidden from the reports and set aside waiting for somebody to deal with them. Christoph Hellwig said that it would be better to keep the pre-existing problems in the patch review, but perhaps mark them differently so that submitters know they are not required to address them. Old problems should not be forced onto new submitters, he said. Mark Brown agreed, saying that submitters should not have to fix a structural problem in order to get a spelling fix in. Hellwig added that removing the pre-existing items is worse, since they are problems that need to be fixed eventually. Gushchin repeated that those problems are collected for people who are interested in fixing them. Zijlstra complained about maintainers who refuse to consider patches until Sashiko reports that it has found no problems. Hellwig, though, said that Sashiko reviews are a good test for submitters; if they know what they are doing, they should be able to explain why a warning is wrong. Thomas Gleixner replied that the worst submitters will just feed the review into their LLM and send the response. Ts'o suggested that the best practice will differ from one subsystem to the next. In larger subsystems, the sub-maintainers may not have the skills to tell whether a given bug report is valid or not; they are having a harder time dealing with false positives. A small subsystem with expert maintainers handles those reports better. The solution is partly cultural, he said; it is necessary to tell people that they can ignore the pre-existing problems. Dave Airlie suggested splitting the report into two emails, one with the review of the patch and a second listing the pre-existing problems. Hellwig shifted the topic slightly by complaining that Sashiko drops most of the recipients from its replies; they should go to everybody, he said, or the thread of the discussion will be broken. David Hildenbrand was quick to disagree, though; in the memory-management subsystem, the Sashiko emails are seen as useful for maintainers, but should not be automatically sent back to the submitter or the mailing list. In a complaint that was heard a few times during the day, he said that submitters spend time submitting multiple versions of a patch set that address comments from Sashiko before human reviewers have a chance to say whether the patch makes sense at all. The Sashiko reviews tend to discourage human reviews in general. His suggestion was that Sashiko should be the last line of defense rather than the first; maintainers should say when the automated review happens. Review practices That led to a discussion on review practices and when human reviewers should get involved with a submission. Ts'o said that, in the ext4 filesystem, it depends on the size of the series and the reputation of the submitter. A single patch from an unknown contributor is likely to be LLM-generated crap, so it ends up low on the prioritized list of work to review. A larger series, though, requires architectural review, so he tends to look mainly at the cover letter and limit comments to the overall design. Jiri Kosina said that deprioritizing unknown contributors is too easy of a solution; in his experience, the patches they submit are often valid. Brown said that proximity to the hardware makes a difference, and that one-off patches to low-level code often have little value. Paolo Abeni said that, in the networking subsystem, there is a complicated scheme for prioritizing reviews that depends on the contributor's reputation, how many reviews that contributor has done, and the reputation of the contributor's employer as well. Airlie warned that tracking reputations raises privacy problems and invites developers to game the system; he understands why that approach has appeal, but a better way is needed. Konstantin Ryabitsev agreed that any reputation system will be gamed. Laurent Pinchart said that some developers are frustrated that they have to justify their work against criticisms from Sashiko while other, LLM-generated patches appear to be accepted immediately. Abeni defended the automated reviews, though, saying that the number of patches introducing bugs has dropped considerably. Zijlstra said that, while reading LLM-generated reviews "shuts my brain down", he still thought that the tool is useful; it finds real problems. Linus speaks At this point Torvalds, who had kept silent until now, spoke up. The problem, he said, is that we are getting increasing numbers of patches from people who do not know the kernel. By pointing the finger at LLMs, maintainers are blaming the wrong thing. LLMs can do a good job, but they are being driven by people who have no clue, and the results are ugly. He suggested maybe delaying reports from Sashiko for 24 hours; that will keep clueless developers from getting an immediate response and cranking out new versions of their work. He has been playing with an LLM on a separate project for several months to learn about the technology, but hadn't used one on the kernel until last week. He took an old patch and had the LLM revise it; the result has made him unwilling to work without an LLM. He plans to post that series at some point. Why bother, he asked, to search for all of the call sites of a function he has just modified, when the tool can fix them all automatically? But, he said, it took six months to set up the tool to not produce bad responses. If you are a competent developer, he said, an LLM makes a great tool, but only after that effort has been put in to set it up. He resisted suggestions to post his LLM-training materials, saying that each developer needs to go through that process separately. In conclusion, he said, arguments about how to deal with people using LLMs are misdirected; instead, developers should be focused on how to use these tools well. Hildenbrand said that Torvalds is an expert, but that we still have to deal with all of the non-experts who are submitting patches; Torvalds said to simply deprioritize them. Sasha Levin suggested putting more information into the repository to try to direct the tools; he later posted a first installment toward building up that information. Ts'o said that it would be useful to try to provide better input for the developers who are willing to put in the effort. Alexei Starovoitov, though, answered that it is not the maintainers' job to teach humans how to work on the kernel. The community is teaching bots by way of the mailing lists, though, and that is reinforcing the problems with rapid reposting of patches. Gushchin said that, eventually, Sashiko may be able to tell a contributor that a patch is a bad idea in general and should not be revised. Greg Kroah-Hartman said that we can expect to be on the receiving end of a firehose for the next 18 months, then we will have fixed most of the bugs and life will get better. Pinchart responded that fixing the bugs is not enough; the kernel is full of bad APIs that are easier to misuse than to use correctly. Kroah-Hartman said that the bugs will eventually be fixed, then there will be space to work on the APIs. Ryabitsev said that problem is that contributing to the kernel has always been gated; it is too hard for many developers to do successfully. LLMs have made the creation of kernel patches easy. Pinchart said that a lot of LLM-using contributors just want to see their name in the changelog; they are not going to stay around, so any effort put into mentoring them is wasted. Torvalds repeated that maintainers should simply deprioritize those contributions. Hildenbrand asked how that could be done; Zijlstra suggested responding to a patch and seeing whether LLM-generated text comes back. Comments that do not evoke a clear human response can simply be ignored. Kroah-Hartman said that is the value of pointing out trivial items, like include files in the wrong order. Christian Brauner said that overly verbose changelogs are often a sign of LLM use. Airlie suggested adding guidance for LLMs that prohibits them from writing changelogs. Levin has been trying to add some of that type of guidance for a while; that effort is likely to be pursued further. There was general agreement that, even if the code is written by an LLM, the accompanying changelog should be written by the human behind the work. Private kernels Brauner said that the work of the kernel community is changing in fundamental ways, and what it means for Linux is unclear. There is increasing interest at companies in maintaining private forks of the kernel and not bothering with upstream. Zijlstra suggested asking Google how well that works; Gleixner added that the fundamental economics around maintaining a kernel have not changed. Brauner said that the developers in the room had grown up in an environment dominated by open-source software, and that working with it could lead to a good career; if that is no longer the case, why should anybody bother contributing back? A number of participants suggested that any company wanting to try its luck with a private fork was welcome to do so. Kroah-Hartman said that the community's goal has always been to make it cheaper to work upstream than to maintain private code. Miguel Ojeda asked whether that was still possible; he knows somebody who has used an LLM to summon forth a complete kernel written in Rust. How can working upstream be cheaper than that? Torvalds said that, if it gets to that point, the community may no longer be viable, but that is not the situation now. Starovoitov said he knew of five working kernels that had been generated in this way; Torvalds answered that there is no point in worrying about them. Tso's said that, if somebody wants to conjure up a fast microkernel for a specific use case, they can do that now, but a general-purpose kernel designed to handle random corner cases is a different story. He thinks that there will be a demand for the Linux kernel for some time yet. Starovoitov stressed the need to understand why there is interest in generating private kernels; Linux, he said, is too full of holes that are not being fixed quickly enough, and contributing to the kernel is too hard. Too hard, or too easy? This was my chance to share a couple of anecdotes I had been saving for this gathering. While running on the unending treadmill that is keeping up with the linux-kernel mailing list, I had recently encountered a series of well over 100 patches, all sent within an hour from a new identity, making significant changes all over the kernel tree. When viewed that way, those patches are the obvious output of an unleashed bot and best ignored, but most maintainers only see a few of them, miss the pattern, and attempt to engage seriously with the sender. So many of those patches are applied. There is an incredible flood of first-time contributors (nearly 800 in 7.3 alone) burying the community in patches. There have been plenty of cases of first-time contributors who make non-trivial changes to multiple subsystems over a short period of time. To me, it is clear that many of these submitters do not understand what they are doing, and they will not be around to fix or maintain those patches. But a lot of that code is getting into the kernel. My fear is that we are building up a collection of code that nobody understands, and that one day we will wake up and find that we have completely lost control of our kernel. Airlie responded that we never really did have control over it. Torvalds said that the time has come to make it harder for new people to contribute code to the kernel. People like Kroah-Hartman have spent years trying to teach people how to contribute; it is time to stop doing that, he said. Ojeda said that there is a need to deprioritize these contributors, but that we still need to find talented people to join our community. That means finding ways to focus on the people who actually matter. For example, the people who take the time to go to conferences are much more likely to stay around. The vast majority of patches from new contributors are not worth it, but some are, and identifying them is hard. Shuah Khan said that she can identify the people who will stick around fairly quickly, and some of the new folks who have come in are excellent. For this reason, she still spends a lot of time with people sending spelling fixes. Hellwig said that developers should be able to use whatever tools they want. For any non-trivial work, there will always be problems to fix; at that point, it is a matter of whether it is possible to have a real conversation with the contributor. Abeni, though, objected that this approach does not scale for the larger subsystems. Generating code Ojeda raised the topic of where generating code with LLMs makes sense. In the presence of a clear specification and a concrete problem, an LLM can create good results, he said. The tools can be good for trying out concepts; it may not even be necessary to look at the resulting code before tossing it and implementing a successful concept properly. Generating tests is another place where LLMs can do well. Brauner said that LLMs can be good for prototyping. Hildenbrand said that the discussion had focused on new contributors, which is fine, but how can we let other maintainers know that it is acceptable to ignore patches from those people? Hellwig said that it is always acceptable to ignore patches; I replied that, for many years, we had been working hard to prevent patches from falling through the cracks. Torvalds suggested adding an AGENTS.md file that makes generating kernel code expensive. He ends every session with a lengthy cleanup pass that takes a couple of hours to run, executing tasks like ensuring that the code matches the comments. That amount of work cannot be done with a free LLM account. I asked whether that risked cutting off bright new developers that we would rather hang onto; Torvalds answered that the kernel project only wants serious developers. That includes having access to enough resources to function in this world. Pinchart said that he has heard from a number of developers who are afraid that they will be forced out of the community; Torvalds replied that it will always possible to write code and send email. The point is filtering out the people who cannot do that on their own. Pinchart asked Torvalds to confirm that he is not trying to push out developers who do not use LLMs; Torvalds agreed that he is not. Pinchart added that it is important to communicate that message to the community. Torvalds added that he does not want to scare off people who want to write code; his message is that you have to either put in the effort to learn, or put a lot of money into an LLM to participate. Airlie expressed a concern that there might not be anything left for those people to write; as soon as an idea is raised, somebody can summon an implementation from an LLM. Alice Ryhl agreed that this could be a problem. Ojeda suggested setting up a way to assign a project to a developer for a period; Hellwig said that the only reason to do that would be for training purposes. Otherwise, why wait when there is an implementation ready? Ojeda said that supporting developers who do not want to use LLMs is also a good reason. Assisted-by Documentation/process/coding-assistants.rst was added to the 7.0 kernel to provide guidance for developers using these tools; among other things, it calls for an Assisted-by tag to be added to the changelog of patches developed with LLM assistance. The 7.3 kernel has seen 18,533 non-merge changesets (a record) added through -rc7, 1,884 (essentially 10%) of them contain Assisted-by tags. The actual number of LLM-assisted patches is surely much higher. In the Summit, I pointed out that huge numbers of contributors are not placing those tags despite using LLMs; sometimes that is the result of ignorance of the rules, while other times contributors want to actively hide their LLM use. But few maintainers are asking contributors about LLM use and ensuring that those tags are present. As a result, Assisted-by provides no useful signal. We should either find a way to enforce the requirement, I suggested, or else just drop it entirely. Airlie said that probably 90% of contributors are using LLMs now. Many of them, he said, fear being caught up in an anti-LLM witch hunt. He suggested adding a requirement that models read all of the kernel's documentation into an AGENTS.md file. Torvalds thought many submitters were simply ashamed to admit that they were using those tools. Gleixner suggested, not entirely seriously, adding a Not-assisted-by tag instead; Arnd Bergmann said he would find that a useful indicator of developers he should put time into helping. Torvalds said that the tag requirement might scare people away from using LLMs, and that he would be happy to drop the requirement; Brauner added that it is pointless now. Khan said that she still found Assisted-by to be useful, but there was a strong consensus in the room that the tag had outlived any purpose it may have had, and that the requirement could be dropped. That said, there was also a general interest in knowing how patches are created. Some would like to see which models were used, or where in the development process they were brought in. Maintainers still want to know if there is a human involved in the development process. There was agreement, though, that this information does not need to be recorded in the changelog; the suggestion came out of the discussion is that this information should be put into the cover letter instead. Security issues and urgent fixes The advent of LLMs has resulted in the discovery of huge numbers of security-relevant bugs, leading to a lot of fixes. Kroah-Hartman, who plays a central role in responding to those bugs, said that there are many more coming. Current tools find a lot of vulnerabilities, he said, but they are also wrong half the time; he has students working on improving that performance. He also has people and funding to help with handling the resulting fixes. We can work through this pile of problems, he said, but it will take a while. That is what the next year of work will be focused on. Levin added that LLMs do two things that are new. One is that they are good at developing an exploit from a patch; the other is that they can be used to monitor mailing lists and figure out which fixes have security implications. The result is machines that are automatically cranking out exploits. As soon as a problem has been detected, he said, any embargo is already over. There are thousands of known exploits out there at the moment. Kroah-Hartman said that the only thing that can be done is to get the fixes into the mainline as quickly as possible. Brauner pointed out that this leads to large pull requests after -rc1, which Torvalds has complained about. Torvalds, though, said that pull requests full of fixes are fine as long as they come from people who he can trust to have verified them to be fixes for real problems. The cost to him of doing a pull is almost zero; it's his job. Pinchart said that, while fixing bugs is good, what is really needed is ways to prevent the addition of new bugs. Kroah-Hartman said that increased use of Rust would help in that regard; many bugs are in error paths, and Rust has better ways of handling those. There is also an effort to scale up the work on hardening C code. Some of that work is landing in the newest versions of the compilers, but developers often do not have easy access to them, and linux-next does not either. Ojeda said there is work underway to increase the availability of prebuilt toolchains that developers can use to test their code. Kroah-Hartman said that security bugs are being immediately copied to maintainers now rather than being kept secret; it is the only way to keep up with the flood. But, he cautioned, maintainers should not be telling their employers about those bugs before they are public; otherwise the project as a whole risks running into trouble with government agencies worldwide. Once a fix has been pushed, though, the embargo ends. Starovoitov said that there are lists of vulnerabilities that have been discovered by LLMs, many of which have reproducers available. He wondered what the best way was to get those fixes into the mainline. Torvalds said that, when there are real kernel developers involved, the most urgent patches can go directly to him, bypassing maintainers and avoiding adding to their workload. Hildenbrand worried that maintainers would lose the opportunity to review fixes in their subsystems, and that they would lose control, but Torvalds answered that reviewing all those fixes just adds stress for everybody involved. Pain points Prior to the Summit, Torvalds asked each of the participants to prepare a one-minute summary of their biggest pain point for the group. These presentations would happen over a half hour, with no discussion until everybody had said their piece. The "no discussion" rule held most (but not all) of the time. In the order they were presented: Kroah-Hartman: subsystems that do not add CC: stable@vger.kernel.org tags to patches, but which still expect the stable team to pick up the important fixes anyway. The stable maintainers are overwhelmed as it is and are not doing that. Pinchart has heard from developers that they submit code, but do not know when their patches have been applied or to which tree. More maintainers should send emails when they apply patches, he said. Eric Biggers: patches that cannot easily be applied, and which do not specify a base to which they can be applied. A lot of patches cannot be properly reviewed without applying them first, he said. Rafael Wysocki: insufficient feedback on patches in general. People often have opinions, but do not always share them. Airlie asked his sub-maintainers; most of them identified him as the biggest pain point. More seriously, it was that the DRM subsystem is still seeing too many regressions. There is a push within the subsystem to move development to GitLab in order to use its CI features; he is not standing in the way because he wants to see how it turns out. Ts'o: prioritization, and having too many things to look at. He would love to add a priority tag to patchwork that maintainers could set to help identify what needs attention first. Ryhl: not knowing how long she needs to wait after sending a version of a patch before concluding that she does not need to worry about problems with it. Me: huge number of patches touch the documentation directory, and it is hard to know which ones I should apply and which to leave to others. A lot of time is spent digging through linux-next to see if patches have been picked up by somebody else. Torvalds said that he often has the same problem. Khan complained about the same problem; it is often not clear who will pick up test patches. Hildenbrand: the high review load. Review cannot just be handed off to a bot; most changes need input from developers. Somehow, the subsystem needs to develop more experts, but it is hard to identify people who can grow in that way. Bergmann said that the review process is breaking down. When he replies to patches, he tries to teach contributors how to do better, but he has become discouraged because people using LLMs do not learn. So now those who might learn are not getting the feedback they need. The opposite problem happens too: a submitter sends 50 versions (literally) of a patch and responds to comments, but Bergmann thinks that the patch should not exist in the first place. Starovoitov: maintainers should not be looking for bugs or coding-style problems; bots will do that now. Instead, reviews should be strictly focused on the "why" of a patch, whether the fix is made in the right place, and is in good taste. Ryabitsev: the last entry in the MAINTAINERS file, titled "THE REST", directs every patch to the linux-kernel mailing list. That generates millions of outgoing emails every day, leading to constant delivery problems. He asked whether that entry could be removed or changed to redirect patches to the patches@vger.kernel.org list. He later submitted a patch to get_maintainer.pl, causing it to only add linux-kernel if no other list has been identified as a recipient for a patch. Levin: subsystems are diverging in their practices, and many now have a manual on how to interact with them. That makes life hard for developers working across subsystems; he would like to see the community come back together. Hellwig: the Sashiko review workflow is broken, causing people to continually resend patches. There is no obvious answer to this problem, but something needs to improve. Brown asked subsystems with tests to actually build and run them so they don't break in linux-next. Kosina: there needs to be a better way to prioritize the handling of submissions. He liked Ts'o's idea, but without using patchwork. Will Deacon: the process is not much fun anymore; maintainers try to explain to contributors how they could improve, but are ignored. Danilo Krummrich does not mind seeing multiple versions of a series in a short time, but submitters are just feeding the Sashiko reviews into their LLM to create those new versions. A way needs to be found to encourage submitters to engage and talk to maintainers. Abeni: the infrastructure is not keeping up with what the subsystem needs. Networking runs its own version of Sashiko, which produces better results, but it can't be run for every networking subsystem. That creates extra friction for maintainers. Eric Dumazet announced that he had just retired, and that all of his pain points have vanished. Gushchin: Sashiko has gone from an experiment to a widely used tool in the community. There is a lot of work involved beyond developing the bot itself; he has to obtain tokens to run it, explain its value to management, and more. He could really use more people and more feedback. He only knows a few kernel subsystems; if people don't tell him about problems with the others, he will never know. Julia Lawall does not know if her work, much of which has involved finding and fixing bugs in the kernel, will have any relevance in the future. Five years ago she would have asked for more feedback from developers, now she isn't sure if it matters. Ojeda: tree-wide refactoring work can be tricky, and the advent of more Rust code seems set to make it harder. Gleixner has spent much of his time looking at design patterns and explaining them in lengthy emails. Developers used to appreciate that work, but more recently it is mostly ignored, and he wonders if it is still worth doing. In the LLM world, people say that they don't have time for design and, besides, the code works. He has spent 25 years doing cleanups, and does not want to merge more stuff that will just have to be cleaned up in the future. Brauner: code removal. The time has come to fix less code and to remove more of it. The idea was that these pain points would be discussed after the presentation, but that did not really happen. Instead, the conversation took a rather different direction. Succession Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. blocks.html_en: The initial topic was automated patch review, and the Sashiko review system in particular. When Sashiko is looking at a specific patch, it often identifies (and reports on) problems that already exist in the code that is modified by that patch. Developers have a love-and-hate relationship with the resulting reports; it is good to know about the bugs, but nobody is thrilled to be given a laundry list of problems in need of fixing, especially if it is seen as an obstacle that must be overcome before they can merge the changes they actually intended to implement.
